books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age
Social Criticism in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: William Graham Sumner, 'The Forgotten Man,' in What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883)
Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889

stimulus.text:
William Graham Sumner, “The Forgotten Man,” in What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883):

“The type and formula of most schemes of philanthropy or humanitarianism is this: A and B put their heads together to decide what C shall be made to do for D. The radical vice of all these schemes, from a sociological point of view, is that C is not allowed a voice in the matter, and his position, character, and interests, as well as the ultimate effects on society through C’s interests, are entirely overlooked. I call C the Forgotten Man.”

Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889:

“The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.”
stimulus.source_note: William Graham Sumner, 'The Forgotten Man,' in What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883); Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889. Both quotations are exact.

stem: How do Sumner and Carnegie differ in these passages?

options.text: Sumner rejects aid paid by others; Carnegie says the rich should give their own wealth
Sumner wants the government to own the railroads, while Carnegie wants private ownership
options.misconception: Sumner opposes government action, and Carnegie says nothing here about railroad ownership.

options.text: Carnegie wants the government to tax all fortunes away, while Sumner wants no taxes at all
options.misconception: Carnegie favors giving by the rich themselves, and Sumner says nothing here about taxes.

options.text: Both men argue that the government should run the whole national economy
options.misconception: Neither passage asks government to run the economy; Sumner opposes government schemes.

rationales.A: Sumner attacks A and B deciding what C must do for D, while Carnegie calls for the rich to administer wealth themselves.
rationales.B: Sumner opposes government action, and Carnegie says nothing about railroad ownership.
rationales.C: Carnegie favors giving by the rich themselves, and Sumner says nothing about taxes here.
rationales.D: Neither passage asks government to run the economy.
rationales.general:
Compare what each man asks of the rich.
1. Sumner attacks schemes where A and B make C pay for D.
2. His target is help given with other people's money.
3. Carnegie instead asks the rich to administer their own wealth for the public good.
4. One man rejects organized giving; the other makes it the rich man's duty.
Remember: two defenders of wealth can still disagree about what the rich owe.
